edges.description: Ingested toxin survives the gut lumen and crosses the proximal intestinal epithelium.
Translocated enterotoxin reaches submucosal mast cells and induces mast-cell degranulation and mediator release.
Mast-cell degranulation, histamine release, and serotonergic signaling activate the vagal pathway required for enterotoxin-induced emesis.
Vagal relay to the vomiting center is the final common pathway for the vomiting-predominant presentation.
The same upper-gastrointestinal toxin signal that activates the emetic reflex produces nausea in the short-incubation syndrome.
Impaired small-intestinal water and electrolyte reabsorption yields toxin-associated diarrhea.
Upper gastrointestinal inflammatory and secretory effects accompany the abdominal cramping syndrome.
Ingesting food that already contains staphylococcal enterotoxin delivers the toxin bolus to the stomach and proximal small intestine.
The shrew model reproduces SEA-induced vomiting and demonstrates that vagal afferent signaling is necessary for the emetic reflex.

Ready-to-eat or cooked food that is contaminated with enterotoxigenic S. aureus and then temperature-abused becomes a vehicle for preformed staphylococcal enterotoxin. Cooking may kill the organism without destroying enough of the heat-stable toxin to prevent intoxication.
